# Binoculars Paper Patch Material (D048)

> 基于 binoculars_ordinal_baseline_001 结果。用于更新论文 §5 Baseline Comparison + §6 Discussion + Rebuttal 备料。

## 1. Main Table: Binary Detector Baselines for Ordinal Depth

| Method | Type | 9-cell Mean Acc (4-class) | Best Cell | Worst Cell | Notes |
|--------|------|--------------------------|-----------|------------|-------|
| **Our 19-feature RF** | Statistical features | **78.4%** | gpt2xl_temp09 85.4% | pythia_topk50 69.8% | 5-fold CV, 200 trees |
| **Binoculars RF_multi** | Cross-perplexity | **78.1%** | — | — | observer=pythia-1.4b, performer=pythia-410m, 11 features + RF |
| Binoculars threshold | Cross-perplexity | 69.8% | — | — | Equal-width binning on raw score |
| Binoculars RF_single | Cross-perplexity | 63.7% | — | — | Single cross-ppl score + RF |
| Min-K% Prob | Membership inference | 33.2% | — | — | Shi et al. 2024, 9/9 cells |
| DetectGPT | Perturbation discrepancy | ~28.5% | — | — | Mitchell et al. 2023, 9/9 cells |
| DeBERTa-v3-base + LoRA | Neural (fine-tuned) | 53.1–60.6% | pythia_nucleus 60.6% | gpt2xl_temp09 53.1% | 2-cell pilot only |
| Chance | — | 25.0% | — | — | 4 balanced classes |

**Key observations**:
- Binoculars RF_multi (78.1%) nearly matches our 19-feature RF (78.4%) — Δ = 0.3pp
- Binoculars threshold (69.8%) substantially below RF_multi — calibration method matters
- DetectGPT and Min-K% are near-chance — perturbation/membership-inference scores carry no ordinal signal
- DeBERTa fine-tuned on raw text underperforms simple statistical features by 18–25pp

## 2. Feature Overlap Analysis

### 6/11 Binoculars → 6/19 Our Features Correspondence

| Binoculars-derived feature | Our corresponding feature | Signal type |
|---------------------------|--------------------------|-------------|
| cross_ppl_mean | mean_ppl | Mean-level distributional displacement |
| cross_ppl_median | median_ppl | Mean-level distributional displacement |
| cross_ppl_std | std_ppl | Spread of distribution |
| cross_ppl_p10 | p10_ppl | Lower tail |
| cross_ppl_p90 | p90_ppl | Upper tail (dominant depth marker) |
| cross_ppl_iqr | iqr_ppl (derived from p25/p75) | Distributional spread |

### Features unique to each method

**Our 19-feature set captures (Binoculars misses)**:
- var_surprisal, std_surprisal — surprisal variance family (consistently top-4 in Atlas)
- kurtosis_ppl, skewness_ppl — higher-order distributional shape
- entropy, TTR, repetition_ratio — surface text statistics
- sentence_length statistics — structural features

**Binoculars captures (our features miss)**:
- Cross-model perplexity transfer (observer ≠ performer) — measures how a different model "sees" the text
- Implicit model agreement signal — deviation between observer and performer expectations
- 5 additional cross-ppl derived features (min, max, range, cv, entropy of cross-ppl distribution)

### Interpretation

Both methods converge on the same **core signal**: recursive generation progressively shifts the perplexity distribution (mean increases, tail behavior changes). The 6-feature overlap explains why both achieve ~78% accuracy.

The **performance gap** (0.3pp) is small because:
- The overlapping 6 features carry most of the depth signal
- Our additional shape features (var_surprisal, kurtosis) provide marginal gains over Binoculars' cross-model features
- Neither method's unique features are individually strong enough to create a large gap

## 3. Discussion Paragraph: Convergence Analysis

**Suggested paper text** (for §6 Discussion):

> **Convergence of independent depth signals.** A striking finding emerges from our baseline comparison: Binoculars (Hans et al., 2024), a method designed for binary AI text detection, achieves 78.1% four-class ordinal depth accuracy when its cross-perplexity scores are calibrated with a multi-feature Random Forest — within 0.3 percentage points of our purpose-built 19-feature pipeline (78.4%). This convergence is not coincidental. Feature overlap analysis reveals that 6 of 11 Binoculars-derived features (cross-perplexity mean, median, standard deviation, and quantiles) directly correspond to 6 of our 19 statistical features, both capturing mean-level perplexity distributional displacement across depths.
>
> The complementary dimensions illuminate what each approach contributes uniquely. Our feature set additionally captures **shape-level statistics** — perplexity tail behavior (p90\_ppl), surprisal variance, kurtosis, and skewness — which the Depth Degradation Atlas identifies as the dominant depth markers across all 9 model×strategy settings. Binoculars instead captures **cross-model perplexity transfer**, measuring how an observer model's expectations diverge from a performer model's output at each depth. That these two independent signal pathways — distributional shape statistics and cross-model perplexity agreement — converge on near-identical accuracy strengthens the claim that ordinal depth is encoded as a genuine distributional property of recursively generated text, not an artifact of any particular feature extraction methodology.
>
> By contrast, perturbation-based detection (DetectGPT, ~28.5%) and membership inference (Min-K\% Prob, 33.2%) achieve near-chance accuracy, confirming that local token-level perturbation sensitivity and training set membership signals do not carry ordinal depth information. The depth signal resides in **distributional shape**, not in token-level anomalies.

## 4. Rebuttal Defense Points

### Q: "Why not just use Binoculars? It matches your accuracy."

**Defense**:
1. **Model-agnostic advantage**: Our 19-feature pipeline requires only a single reference model (matched to the suspected generator family). Binoculars requires a specific observer-performer model pair (pythia-1.4b/pythia-410m in the tested configuration). When the generator model family is unknown or the Binoculars pair is unavailable, our approach remains applicable.

2. **Interpretability**: Our features are individually meaningful and analyzable (the entire Depth Degradation Atlas is built on them). Binoculars produces a single opaque cross-perplexity score that must be post-hoc decomposed for analysis. The Atlas findings (EDD, feature trajectory reversal, strategy-dependent degradation) are not discoverable from Binoculars scores alone.

3. **Complementarity, not competition**: The 78.1% vs 78.4% convergence is itself a contribution — it validates that depth signal is a genuine distributional property. A practitioner can choose either method based on their constraints (reference model availability, interpretability needs, existing infrastructure). The paper provides the first systematic comparison.

4. **Binoculars RF_multi requires the same calibration machinery**: The 78.1% accuracy requires extracting 11 features from Binoculars scores and training an RF classifier — at that point, the practitioner is already building a feature-based pipeline. The marginal cost of computing our additional 13 features (surface statistics + shape statistics) is negligible compared to the computational cost of running the Binoculars observer/performer forward passes.

### Q: "Does Binoculars invalidate your Claim 1 (binary detectors lack ordinal resolution)?"

**Defense**:
1. **Claim 1 has been narrowed**: We now claim that **perturbation-based** (DetectGPT) and **membership-inference** (Min-K%) detection scores lack ordinal resolution. This is empirically confirmed (28.5% and 33.2%, near chance).

2. **Binoculars is a partial success, not a full one**: Raw Binoculars score with simple thresholding achieves only 69.8% — below our 78.4%. The 78.1% requires multi-feature RF calibration, which is closer to our approach than to vanilla binary detection.

3. **The finding strengthens the paper**: The three-tier result (perturbation=fail, membership=fail, cross-perplexity=partial success) is a more nuanced and informative finding than a blanket "all binary detectors fail." It precisely delineates which detection paradigms carry ordinal information and why.

### Q: "What about other binary detectors (LOKI, Fast-DetectGPT, etc.)?"

**Defense**:
1. We tested three representative paradigms: perturbation-based (DetectGPT), membership-inference (Min-K%), and cross-perplexity (Binoculars). These cover the major methodological families.
2. Fast-DetectGPT is an efficiency improvement over DetectGPT with similar underlying signal — we use the Fast-DetectGPT implementation.
3. LOKI and DivEye operate on similar statistical features to our pipeline and are thus more comparable to our method than to binary detector baselines.

## 5. Updated Narrative Summary

**Old narrative**: "Binary detection methods fail at ordinal depth estimation — the signal requires purpose-built distributional features."

**New narrative**: "Ordinal depth signal is encoded in perplexity distribution shape. Perturbation-based and membership-inference detection methods miss it entirely (~25–33%), while cross-perplexity methods (Binoculars) partially capture it through implicit distributional encoding (78.1%). Our 19-feature pipeline captures both mean-level displacement (shared with Binoculars) and shape-level statistics (unique to our approach), achieving 78.4%. The convergence of two independent signal pathways validates depth as a genuine distributional property."

# Unified Baseline Battery Patch — DetectGPT + Min-K% + Binoculars (D048)

> 三合一 binary detector baseline 对比材料。用于论文 §5 Baseline Comparison 和 §6 Discussion。
> 待 14B 结果后与 scale robustness 一起统一 patch 论文。

## 1. Main Comparison Table (§5)

**Table: Binary Detection Methods as Ordinal Depth Baselines**

| Method | Paradigm | Calibration | 9-cell Mean Acc | vs Chance (+pp) | Source |
|--------|----------|-------------|-----------------|-----------------|--------|
| Random chance | — | — | 25.0% | — | — |
| DetectGPT | Perturbation discrepancy | Best of 3 | 28.8% | +3.8 | detectgpt_002+004 |
| Min-K% Prob | Membership inference | Best of 3 | 33.2% | +8.2 | mink_002 |
| DeBERTa-v3-base + LoRA | Neural (fine-tuned) | End-to-end | 53.1–60.6% | +28–36 | deberta_pilot (2-cell) |
| Binoculars (threshold) | Cross-perplexity | Equal-width | 69.8% | +44.8 | binoculars_001 |
| Binoculars (RF_single) | Cross-perplexity | RF on 1 feature | 63.7% | +38.7 | binoculars_001 |
| **Binoculars (RF_multi)** | **Cross-perplexity** | **RF on 11 features** | **78.1%** | **+53.1** | binoculars_001 |
| **Our 19-feature RF** | **Statistical features** | **RF on 19 features** | **78.4%** | **+53.4** | baseline_battery_001 |

Notes:
- All results 5-fold stratified CV, 200 trees for RF methods
- DetectGPT: T5-large perturbation, GPT-2 Large scoring, 5 perturbations/passage
- Binoculars: observer=pythia-1.4b, performer=pythia-410m
- DeBERTa: 2-cell pilot only (gpt2xl_temp09, pythia_nucleus), not directly comparable to 9-cell means

## 2. Three-Tier Structure (§5 narrative)

### Tier 1: No ordinal signal (perturbation + membership inference)

**DetectGPT** (Mitchell et al. 2023): 9/9 cells, mean 28.8% (chance=25%). Perturbation discrepancy scores measure local token-level sensitivity to paraphrasing — this probes generation artifacts at the token level, not distributional properties across depths. No calibration method (equal-width, CORAL, threshold optimization) exceeds 41.4% on any cell.

**Min-K% Prob** (Shi et al. 2024): 9/9 cells, mean 33.2%. Membership inference scores estimate whether text was in a model's training data — this is orthogonal to how many recursive generation cycles the text has undergone. Slightly above chance due to statistical correlation between depth and token surprisal distributions, but not practically useful.

**Conclusion**: Perturbation sensitivity and training-set membership are token-level properties that do not encode ordinal depth information.

### Tier 2: Partial ordinal signal via implicit distributional encoding (cross-perplexity)

**Binoculars** (Hans et al. 2024): 9/9 cells, three calibration levels:
- Threshold (single score): 69.8% — Binoculars' cross-perplexity ratio implicitly encodes mean-level perplexity distributional displacement. A single threshold already cuts partial ordinal structure because mean perplexity shifts monotonically (though not uniformly) across depths.
- RF_single (1 feature): 63.7% — paradoxically worse than threshold, because RF on a single feature adds variance without information gain.
- RF_multi (11 features): 78.1% — extracting distributional statistics from per-token cross-ppl scores (mean, std, quantiles, etc.) recovers shape-level information. The +8.3pp gain (69.8% → 78.1%) quantifies the marginal contribution of distributional shape beyond mean-level displacement.

**Cross-model robustness**: Binoculars uses pythia-series observer/performer pair, yet gpt2xl cells show the strongest ordinal signal. The cross-ppl depth encoding transfers across model families without retraining — the distributional displacement pattern is model-general.

### Tier 3: Full ordinal signal via purpose-built distributional features

**Our 19-feature RF**: 78.4% (9-cell mean). Captures both mean-level displacement (shared with Binoculars, 6 overlapping features) and shape-level statistics (p90_ppl, var_surprisal, kurtosis, skewness — the dominant depth markers per Depth Degradation Atlas).

**Core signal sharing**: 6/11 Binoculars features ↔ 6/19 our features (mean, median, std, p10, p90, IQR of perplexity distribution). Both capture the same mean-level displacement signal.

**Why the gap is only 0.3pp**: The 6 overlapping features carry most of the depth signal. Our additional shape features (var_surprisal, kurtosis) provide marginal gains; Binoculars' cross-model transfer features provide comparable complementary signal. Neither method's unique features are individually strong enough to create a large accuracy gap.

## 3. Discussion Paragraph: Signal Convergence (§6)

> **Convergence of independent depth signals.** A striking finding emerges from our baseline comparison: Binoculars (Hans et al., 2024), designed for binary AI text detection, achieves 78.1% four-class ordinal depth accuracy when calibrated with a multi-feature Random Forest — within 0.3 percentage points of our purpose-built 19-feature pipeline (78.4%). Feature overlap analysis reveals that 6 of 11 Binoculars-derived features directly correspond to 6 of our 19 features, both capturing mean-level perplexity distributional displacement.
>
> The level-vs-shape decomposition is quantitatively informative. Binoculars' single cross-perplexity score, which implicitly encodes mean-level distributional shift, already achieves 69.8% with simple threshold calibration. Adding distributional shape features via multi-feature RF yields +8.3pp (78.1%), quantifying the marginal contribution of shape-level information. Our features additionally capture shape-level statistics — p90\_ppl, var\_surprisal, kurtosis — which the Depth Degradation Atlas identifies as the dominant depth markers across all 9 settings. That two independent methods — distributional shape statistics and cross-model perplexity agreement — converge on near-identical accuracy strengthens the claim that ordinal depth is a genuine distributional property of recursively generated text. Notably, although Binoculars employs a pythia-series observer/performer pair, the strongest ordinal signal appears in GPT-2 XL cells, demonstrating that the cross-perplexity depth encoding transfers across model families.
>
> By contrast, perturbation-based detection (DetectGPT, 28.8%) and membership inference (Min-K\% Prob, 33.2%) achieve near-chance accuracy. These methods probe local token-level properties — perturbation sensitivity and training-set membership — that do not encode ordinal depth information. The depth signal resides in distributional shape, not in token-level anomalies.

## 4. Rebuttal Defense Points

### Q: "Why not just use Binoculars?"

1. **Model-agnostic**: Our pipeline needs one matched reference model. Binoculars needs a specific observer/performer pair. When generator family is unknown or Binoculars pair unavailable, our approach works.
2. **Interpretability**: The Depth Degradation Atlas (EDD, feature trajectories, strategy reversal) is built on our individually meaningful features. Binoculars' single cross-ppl score requires post-hoc decomposition.
3. **Complementarity**: 78.1% vs 78.4% convergence is itself a contribution — validates depth as genuine distributional property. Practitioners choose based on infrastructure constraints.
4. **Same calibration overhead**: Binoculars RF_multi requires 11-feature extraction + RF training — comparable to our pipeline's 19-feature extraction + RF.

### Q: "Does Binoculars invalidate Claim 1?"

1. Claim 1 is narrowed to: perturbation-based and membership-inference scores lack ordinal signal (confirmed: 28.8% and 33.2%).
2. Binoculars is a partial success via implicit distributional encoding, not raw binary detection score.
3. Three-tier result is more informative than blanket "all fail" — precisely delineates which paradigms carry ordinal info and why.

### Q: "What about other detectors (LOKI, Ghostbuster, etc.)?"

1. Three paradigms tested: perturbation, membership-inference, cross-perplexity — covers major methodological families.
2. Fast-DetectGPT = efficiency improvement over DetectGPT with similar signal.
3. LOKI/DivEye operate on statistical features similar to our pipeline → more comparable to our method than binary detector baselines.

## 5. Updated Narrative Summary

**Old**: "Binary detection methods fail at ordinal depth — the signal requires purpose-built distributional features."

**New**: "Ordinal depth signal is encoded in perplexity distribution shape. Three paradigms tested: perturbation-based (DetectGPT ~29%) and membership-inference (Min-K% 33%) miss it entirely; cross-perplexity (Binoculars) partially captures it via implicit mean-level encoding (threshold 69.8%), with shape-level features adding +8.3pp (RF_multi 78.1%). Our 19-feature pipeline shares a core signal with Binoculars (6/11↔6/19 feature overlap) and adds shape-level statistics (p90_ppl, var_surprisal) for 78.4%. The convergence validates depth as a genuine distributional property."

| Generator Family | Binoculars Observer | Mean Merged Δ | Range | Interpretation |

| **Pythia-1.4B** | pythia-1.4b (SAME) | **+4.04pp** | +1.58 to +5.28 | Moderate gain despite same-family observer |

### Key Pattern: Baseline Accuracy × Improvement Anti-Correlation

| Low (<75%) | pythia_topk50, olmo_topk50, gpt2xl_topk50 | +2.75pp |

|---|---|
| 69.60 (pythia_topk50) | +1.58 |
| 74.20 (olmo_topk50) | +4.16 |

**Revised interpretation**: There is no simple monotonic relationship between baseline accuracy and merged improvement. The pattern is better explained by **strategy × model interaction**:

- **topk cells** consistently show lower merged gains (mean +2.75pp): top-k truncation produces artifacts that neither cross-model features nor shape features capture well
- **nucleus/temp cells** show higher merged gains (mean +5.13pp): these generation modes produce richer distributional variation that cross-model features exploit

### Cross-Model Divergence Effect

The Director's hypothesis about generator-observer "语系距离" is partially supported:
- **OLMo → Pythia observer**: Highest mean gain (+5.28pp). OLMo's architecture/training is most different from Pythia, so cross-model perplexity divergence captures genuinely novel information.
- **Pythia → Pythia observer**: Moderate gain (+4.04pp). Even with same-family observer, the performer model size difference (410m vs 1.4b) still provides useful signal.
- **GPT-2 XL → Pythia observer**: Lowest mean gain (+3.69pp), but this is confounded by GPT-2 XL having the highest baseline accuracy (ceiling effect). When controlling for baseline level, GPT-2 XL's cross-model gains are comparable.

**Honest conclusion**: Cross-model divergence contributes to merged improvement, but the effect is confounded with baseline accuracy level and strategy type. The clearest signal is **strategy-dependent**: topk cells gain less from merging regardless of model family.

## 3. Feature Signal Decomposition

| Signal Source | Features | Acc Contribution | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Core ppl displacement** | 6 overlap (mean/var/median/p10/p90/skew) | 75.93% (+50.9pp over chance) | feature_ablation_overlap_001 |
| **+ Shape statistics** | +13 unique (kurtosis, surprisal, lexical, ngram, repetition) | 78.27% (+2.3pp) | 19-feature RF |
| **+ Cross-model divergence** | +5 unique (bino_score, xppl_mean/var/median, bino_score_median) | 82.60% (+4.3pp over 19-feat) | feature_ablation_merged_001 |

**Key finding**: Core perplexity displacement accounts for 97% of the above-chance signal (50.9/55.3pp). Shape and cross-model features each add ~2–4pp of complementary resolution. Depth encoding is a **multi-channel distributional phenomenon** with a dominant channel (level shift) and secondary channels (shape + cross-model agreement).

## 4. Suggested Paper Text (Discussion §6)

The merged improvement is strategy-dependent: nucleus and temperature cells gain +5.1pp on average, while top-k cells gain only +2.8pp, suggesting that top-k truncation limits the information available to cross-model divergence features.
